title: Fully Dynamic Coreset Spectral Clustering
one_liner: Keep a changing graph clustered fast by sampling edges lazily only when someone asks for cluster membership.
lead: Spectral clustering groups nodes in a network into communities by looking at the graph's structure. But real graphs change all the time — nodes and edges appear and disappear. This paper presents a data structure that updates the grouping in milliseconds when the graph changes, because it does not need to recompute everything — it only recomputes the parts that matter. It also answers "which cluster is this node in?" instantly, because it samples only the boundary edges that define the clusters, not all edges.

problem.h2: The problem: clustering keeps breaking when graphs change
paras: A graph is just nodes (dots) and edges (connections between them). Spectral clustering groups nodes into clusters by analyzing the graph's structure — it finds dense regions where many nodes connect to each other, and sparse cuts where few edges cross.

But real graphs are alive. Social networks gain and lose friendships. Collaboration networks add and remove authors. Every time the graph changes, the old clusters become stale. A naive approach: rerun the clustering algorithm from scratch each time. On a large graph with millions of nodes, this is far too slow — you might wait seconds or minutes just to answer one query.
The naive approach recomputes everything. The hidden cost is that most of the old clusters are still correct — you are throwing away correct work and redoing it.

callout.html: When graphs change constantly, reclustering from scratch wastes time recomputing clusters that barely changed.

steps.text: Keep a tree that holds edges, but do not compute clusters yet.
When an edge is added or removed, update its position in the tree.
Someone asks: what cluster is node X in?
Walk the tree and sample (pick) edges that matter for node X's cluster.
Report which cluster node X belongs to, using the sampled edges.

object.h2: What the paper changes: sampling strategy
paras: Instead of storing all edges or precomputing all clusters, the paper's data structure stores edges in a tree and samples them (picks a subset) only when someone asks for a cluster. By sampling only the boundary edges (the ones that cross between clusters), the method avoids wasting computation on edges deep inside clusters that cannot affect the answer. This shift makes updates instant and queries fast because the total work per change is much smaller.

hidden.name: Approximation error
paras: Because the method samples edges instead of using all of them, the clusters are approximate — not exactly optimal, but close enough. The paper tracks how far the sampled cluster assignment can drift from the true optimal clustering. This error grows with how many edges are hidden (not sampled), and shrinks as you sample more edges.

The paper bounds this error using a parameter epsilon (a small number you set). If epsilon is 0.1, the clusters are at most 10 percent worse than optimal. If epsilon is 0.01, they are much closer. The paper ensures that the error bounds hold even as the graph changes over time.

heat.caption: Darker means more confidence; hidden edges introduce approximation error.

reads.html: Approximation error tells you how wrong the clusters can be when you skip edges.
The paper bounds the clustering quality loss by a ratio of (1 + epsilon) / (1 - epsilon), where epsilon is a parameter you choose.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: sample only boundary edges
paras: You do not need all edges to figure out clusters; you need only the edges that cross cluster boundaries. The paper uses a Just-in-Time Sampling Tree, which is a tree that organizes edges by whether they are boundary edges or interior edges. When an edge is added or removed, you update the tree by moving it a few nodes up or down — a small constant-time task. When you query which cluster a node belongs to, you walk the tree and sample (pick) only the edges most likely to tell you which side of a boundary the node sits on. Edges that are deep inside clusters are skipped because they do not help define the boundary.

This works because spectral clustering finds clusters by looking at where edges are sparse. A graph with a million nodes might have a hundred million edges, but only a small fraction cross cluster boundaries. By sampling smartly, the method identifies those boundary edges without looking at all the edges. Updates touch only the tree, not precomputed clusters, so they finish quickly. Queries sample only the edges needed to answer the question, so they also finish quickly. The total cost per change is low because neither updates nor queries touch the full edge set.

stages.s: Graph changes: add or remove edge
Update tree by moving edge up or down
Query arrives: which cluster is node X?
Sample only boundary edges from tree

math.h2: The key equation: bounded approximation error
math.words: The quality of the clustering is at most (1 + epsilon) divided by (1 - epsilon) times the best possible clustering, where epsilon is a small number you choose.
symbols: How much worse the sampled clustering is compared to the optimal
A small number you choose, like 0.1 or 0.01, that controls the trade-off
The loss from sampling too few edges
The noise tolerance in the clustering

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: If you set epsilon = 0.1, then quality_loss <= (1 + 0.1) / (1 - 0.1) = 1.1 / 0.9 = 1.222
This means your clustering is at most 22.2% worse than the absolute best.
If you set epsilon = 0.01, then quality_loss <= (1 + 0.01) / (1 - 0.01) = 1.01 / 0.99 = 1.020
Now it is only 2% worse — much better, but sampling takes longer.

math.note: Smaller epsilon means better clusters, but longer query times because you sample more edges.

charts.title: Naive method: recompute each time
charts.note: Recomputing the full clustering on every change is very slow.

charts.title: This paper: Just-in-Time Trees
charts.note: Updates take 5 time units: move one edge in the tree. Queries take 18 time units: sample boundary edges and compute cluster. Naive re-clustering takes 97 time units: recompute clusters from all edges. The method is so much faster because it avoids the large cost of full recomputation.

items.b: If you set epsilon too large
items.html: Queries run fast but clusters become very approximate and unreliable. You lose quality.

items.b: If the graph is extremely dense
items.html: Most edges are boundary edges, so sampling does not save much time. The method works best on sparse graphs.
A few hub nodes with thousands of edges are harder to cluster accurately; the method assumes degree is bounded.
On sparse real-world graphs (social networks, collaboration graphs), the method is both fast and accurate.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a demo that generates a graph with 1000 nodes and 10000 edges (sparse, with clear clusters). Add 10 edges, one at a time, and remove 10 edges. After each change, query for the cluster of 100 random nodes. Measure the update time and query time for each step. Compare against naive re-clustering. Show that updates are 10x faster because the tree changes only locally, and queries are answered in milliseconds because only boundary edges are sampled, not all edges.
demo.metric_eq: Speedup = (time for naive recompute) / (time for update + query)
demo.closing: The demo must make it clear that updates are nearly free and queries are instant, even when the graph changes constantly.
